newsitem.title: USA: Columbia chairman Scott looks vulnerable.
newsitem.headline: Columbia chairman Scott looks vulnerable.

text.p: If Columbia/HCA Healthcare Corp chairman Richard Scott has not resigned, he looks vulnerable to ouster soon, said Wall Street analysts Friday.
"It certainly wouldn't surprise anyone," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.

The Tennesseean newspaper in Nashville, Tenn., quoted Associated Press reports Friday that said Scott has resigned as chairman of the board of the largest U.S. for-profit hospital company. He is also president and chief executive.

The newspaper said members of the 10-person Columbia board met into the late hours of Thursday night to discuss concerns about a widening federal investigation of the Nashville-based company and Scott's handling of it, as well as other issues.
The newspaper said that the AP reported Scott was "out as Columbia/HCA chairman."
The company did not respond to inquiries seeking comment on Friday.
"Speculation about a senior management change at Columbia is gathering momentum," said Bear Stearns healthcare analyst Albert Rice.
At the meeting Thursday, the Columbia board also may have discussed a possible merger of the company with Tenet HealthCare Corp, the second-largest U.S. for-profit hospital firm, it was reported.

Analysts said a Columbia-Tenet deal, while fraught with difficulties, may occur and could offer a way out for both Scott and the embattled company he built from scratch into a healthcare titan with nearly $20 billion in 1996 revenues.
Jeffrey Barbakow, chairman and chief executive of Santa Barbara, Calif.-based Tenet, guided the company through the end of a difficult period involving another government probe.

Tenet was formerly called National Medical Enterprises, a hospital company that in 1992 was sued by several large insurers alleging that NME had filed hundreds of millions of dollars of fraudulent claims for psychiatric care. NME settled the lawsuits and in June 1993 hired Barbakow, an investment banker, to come in and clean up the company.
NME's founders were ousted, but just two months after Barbakow took over, hundreds of federal agents raided NME headquarters and seized paper related to the alleged fraud.

Under Barbakow's leadership, NME sold off all its psychiatric facilities and rehabilitation hospitals in 1993 and 1994. Proceeds from the sale helped cover NME's payment of about $380 million in federal and state fines to end the sweeping three-year government probe into allegations of insurance fraud, kickbacks and psychiatric patient abuse.

In 1995, NME changed its name to Tenet -- a moniker meant to evoke the company's new code of principles and values -- and embarked on a series of acquisitions. After integrating its January purchase of OrNda HealthCorp, Tenet will boast annual revenues of about $8.5 billion.
If Tenet and Columbia were to merge, it is unclear who would end up running things, analysts said.

"I don't think it would have to be Jeffrey Barbakow. There are some good people on the Columbia board. Tom Frist and Clayton McWhorter are both well-regarded executives. Either of them could step in if something were to happen," said Hilliard Lyons healthcare analyst Stephen O'Neil.
Said another analyst who asked not to be named: "Remember, Barbakow is not an operations guy. He's an investment banker."
